claim: Helium flux selection and backgrounds (first 30 months): collection time counts only seconds in normal operating conditions with AMS within 40 degrees of the local zenith, data-acquisition live time above 50% and the ISS outside the South Atlantic Anomaly (constant at 6.29x10^7 s above 30 GV); downward-going events with an inner-tracker track of charge compatible with Z=2 (1.7 < Z < 2.5) give 1.7x10^9 events; the track must pass L1 to L9 with chi^2/d.o.f. < 10 in the bending coordinate, and the charge measured by L1, upper TOF, lower TOF and L9 must be compatible with Z=2 to remove interacting candidates; the rigidity must exceed 1.2 times the maximum geomagnetic cutoff in the field of view (IGRF backtracing to 50 Earth radii), leaving 5.0x10^7 events; the proton contamination is below 10^-4 and helium produced by heavier nuclei interacting at the top of AMS below 10^-3, both subtracted with their uncertainties in the systematic errors; the flux is N/(A eps T dR) in 68 bins, with a trigger efficiency of 95-99.5% (Monte Carlo agrees within 0.5%) and a migration correction of +15% at 2 GV, +5% at 3 GV, -5% at 300 GV and -19% at 3 TV
limitations: Main article only; choices of this analysis. It requires tracks through L1 and L9, unlike the L1-only daily helium selection (C54) and the 30-degree Bartels-rotation nuclei selection (C56).

claim: Helium flux systematic-error ledger (first 30 months): trigger efficiency (below 0.2% under 100 GV, 1% at 3 TV, limited by the 1% prescaled sample); geomagnetic cutoff factor varied from 1.0 to 1.4 (below 0.1%); acceptance from Monte Carlo corrected for data/MC differences (below 2% total correction; systematic below 1% under 200 GV, 1.4% at 3 TV); helium inelastic interaction with detector material, measured with a survival-probability method using a horizontal-pointing sample and Glauber-Gribov cross sections scaled by 1.05-1.20 (1% under 100 GV, 2% at 3 TV); 3He/4He composition (0.3%, varying the ratio from 0 to 0.2); rigidity resolution function, varying the Gaussian core by 5% and the non-Gaussian tail amplitude by 10% (below 1% under 400 GV, 3.5% at 3 TV); difference between two unfolding procedures (0.25% at 2 GV, below 0.1% from 2.5 to 200 GV, 0.4% at 3 TV); rigidity scale from tracker misalignment and the field map (below 0.6% to 100 GV, 6% at 3 TV); bin widths changed by factors of 2 and 4 gave an uncertainty within the assigned errors
limitations: Main article only; numbers are those of this helium analysis and must not be applied to other species or periods.

claim: Helium rigidity resolution and its verification (first 30 months): the resolution function has a Gaussian core with width sigma/(1/R) = 9% at 10 GV, 14% at 100 GV, 20% at 400 GV and 64% at 2 TV, and non-Gaussian tails beyond 2.5 sigma of 3% at 10 GV, 6% at 100 GV, 11% at 400 GV and 8% at 2 TV; it comes from simulation and was checked with data in four ways (layer coordinate residuals against the fit from the other layers, L1/L9 residuals against the inner-tracker fit, comparison of rigidities from L1-L8 and L2-L9, and a RICH-velocity-based resolution up to 20 GV), giving a maximum detectable rigidity of 3.2 +- 0.16 TV and a 10% uncertainty on the tail amplitude
limitations: Main article only; helium-specific and time-period-specific. Illustrates why tails need an independent check and why the core width alone is not the validation.

claim: Helium, carbon and oxygen flux paper (first five years): the same selection as the helium paper with 40-degree pointing, 8.5x10^10 events collected and a collection time constant at 1.23x10^8 s above 30 GV; 90x10^6 helium events with purity above 99.9%; 67 rigidity bins from 2.2 GV to 3.0 TV with identical bin widths for all nuclei; unfolding done independently for He, C and O (corrections +14% at 3 GV, +6% at 5 GV, -4% at 150 GV and -6% at 3 TV for carbon); systematic terms are background, trigger (below 0.7%), cutoff factor varied 1.0-1.4 (below 0.1% under 30 GV), acceptance (reconstruction and selection below 1%), inelastic cross sections (below 2.2% for C and 2.7% for O to 100 GV, 3% and 3.5% at 3 TV), resolution function (below 1% under 300 GV, 4% at 3 TV, core varied by 5% and tails by 10%) and absolute rigidity scale; maximum detectable rigidity 3.2 TV for He, 3.7 TV for C and 3.4 TV for O with 5% uncertainty
location: Event selection, Analysis and Results sections

scope.text: He, C, O; 2.2 GV-3 TV; first five years
scope.analysis: He, C, O flux selection and systematics

limitations: Main article only; supplemental tables not read. The abstract-level result (identical rigidity dependence above 60 GV, hardening above 200 GV) is stated in the abstract, not here.

claim: Tracker rigidity measurement (review): tracks are found with a cellular-automaton track-finding algorithm and fitted with a Kalman filter that accounts for energy loss and multiple scattering; below 20 GV the rigidity resolution Delta R/R is 0.1; the maximum detectable rigidity is 2.0 TV for protons, 3.2 TV for helium, 3.7 TV for carbon, 3.4 TV for oxygen and 3.7 TV for iron; the simulation was compared with 400 GeV/c test-beam protons over five orders of magnitude in the inverse-rigidity distribution, including tails, and, beyond the beam energy, with ISS data by comparing the rigidity from L1-L8 with that from L2-L9 for protons in 1130-1800 GV

scope.text: Tracker rigidity performance and validation; nine-layer configuration; review of the first seven years
scope.range: below 20 GV for the resolution; MDR for the listed nuclei
scope.analysis: tracker rigidity resolution, MDR and validation

limitations: Review-level summary (Phys. Rept. 894); section 1.2 only was read, other chapters were not. Consistent with C21 and C61 for the overlapping numbers (helium MDR 3.2 TV); the detector configuration is the nine-layer L1-L9 case, and the MDR values are not for other track configurations.

claim: Absolute rigidity scale (review): the rigidity scale is the largest systematic at the highest energies for all Z; a coherent inner-tracker shift below 0.5 micrometre is sufficient to shift the scale by 10% at 1 TV; the in-flight shift is measured by comparing 1/|R| from the tracker with 1/E from the ECAL for electrons and positrons in 72 energy bins from 2 to 300 GeV, modelling each bin's 1/|R|-1/E distribution as a Gaussian plus an exponentially modified Gaussian and fitting shift parameters s+ and s- by unbinned likelihood, with s=(s+ - s-)/2; a time-dependent correction was derived by dividing the first seven years into four intervals
location: Section 1.2.3, Determination of tracker absolute rigidity scale and alignment

scope.text: AMS tracker absolute rigidity scale determination; May 2011 to May 2018

limitations: Review-level summary; section 1.2 only was read. This is one collaboration method with a stated dependence on ECAL energy calibration, not a general recipe, and the residual accuracy statement after the truncated passage was not transcribed.

claim: Charge-sign identification and charge confusion (review): charge confusion, meaning particles reconstructed with the wrong charge sign because of finite tracker resolution or interactions in the detector material, is measured with a boosted-decision-tree charge-confusion estimator Lambda_CC built from E/p, the track chi^2/d.o.f., momenta from different layer combinations, the number of hits near the track and the TOF and tracker charge measurements (positrons near +1, charge-confusion electrons near -1); after TRD and ECAL selection, the confusion in data comes from a template fit of the Lambda_CC distribution in the positive and negative rigidity samples, with the confusion fraction N_cc/(N_cc + N) and the MC fraction defined as electrons reconstructed with positive rigidity after the same cuts; the electron charge-confusion fraction is below 8% up to 1 TeV and is well reproduced by the simulation; similar methods separate antiprotons and antideuterons from proton and deuteron backgrounds

scope.text: electron and positron charge confusion; energy up to 1 TeV

limitations: Review-level summary; section 1.2 only was read. The 8% bound is a review statement for the electron sample after that selection, not a general charge-confusion rate; the antiproton and antideuteron methods are only named, not described.
